courseTitle: Physics 2: Fluids, Heat, Electricity, Light and Atoms
title: Charges in a Uniform Field
short: Between parallel plates E is uniform, so a charge feels a constant force qE and moves like a projectile.
trouble: Students forget that an electron is pushed opposite to the field.

blocks.html: Between two large, flat, oppositely charged plates, the electric field is the same everywhere: the same size and the same direction. A charge there feels a constant force, so it moves just like a ball in projectile motion, with the electric force playing the part of gravity.

Each plate is a sheet of charge whose field does not weaken with distance (for points close to a large sheet). Between the plates the two fields point the same way and add; outside they point opposite ways and cancel. So the field is uniform between the plates and nearly zero outside. A uniform field gives a constant force $qE$ and a constant acceleration $a = qE/m$, and all of constant-acceleration kinematics applies.

In a uniform field, $a = \dfrac{qE}{m}$, constant. A positive charge accelerates along $\vec E$; an electron accelerates opposite to $\vec E$. A charge entering sideways follows a parabola: constant speed along the plates, constant acceleration across them.

blocks.name: ph-efield

opts.task: Change the voltage and the entry speed. Watch the parabola.

blocks.cap: An electron between charged plates bends toward the positive plate, against the field.

blocks.title: A proton's acceleration
blocks.q: Find the acceleration of a proton in a uniform field of $2.0 \times 10^{4}\,\text{N/C}$.
steps: About $10^{11}$ times $g$, which is why gravity is ignored here.

blocks.title: Bending an electron beam
blocks.q: An electron enters the gap between plates $4.0\,\text{cm}$ long at $2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m/s}$, moving parallel to them. The field is $500\,\text{N/C}$. How far sideways is it pushed?

blocks.title: A floating oil drop
blocks.q: An oil drop of mass $3.27 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{kg}$ hangs at rest in a downward field of $1.0 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N/C}$. What is its charge?
steps: At rest: the electric force balances the weight, $|q|E = mg$, so $|q| = \dfrac{(3.27 \times 10^{-15})(9.8)}{1.0 \times 10^{5}} = 3.20 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.
That is $2e$. The force must point up, against the downward field, so the drop is negative: $q = -2e$. Millikan found charges like this were always whole multiples of $e$.

blocks.html: Forgetting that an electron is pushed opposite to the field. $\vec F = q\vec E$, and for an electron $q$ is negative. In a field pointing up, an electron accelerates down. Check: an electron always moves toward the positive plate.
